# LNT v5

> LNT is LLVM's performance-monitoring server. Build bots submit benchmark
> results to it; it stores them as time series and serves them back so that
> performance changes can be found, investigated and tracked. This instance
> exposes everything it knows through the REST API described below.

This document orients an automated client -- an agent or a script -- that needs
to drive this API. It is deliberately short: it gives the shape of the system
and the handful of rules that are not guessable, and leaves the per-endpoint
detail to the machine-readable specification.

## Documentation

- [OpenAPI specification](/api/openapi.json): every endpoint, parameter,
  request body, response body and status code this instance can produce. This
  is the authoritative reference; read it before constructing a request.
- [Interactive documentation](/api/docs): the same specification, rendered for
  a human.
- [API index](/api): links to the suite list and to both of the above.

Both documentation routes are public and ignore any `Authorization` header, so
a caller holding a broken token can still read them.

## Concepts

- **Test suite** -- a namespace with a schema of its own. Nearly every endpoint
  lives under `/api/suites/{testsuite}/`, and nothing is shared between suites:
  two suites may hold machines of the same name and they are different machines.
  Suites are few, and `GET /api/suites` returns all of them with their schemas.
- **Schema** -- a suite declares its `metrics`, `machine_fields` and
  `commit_fields` up front. Each entry has a `name` and a `type`, one of `real`,
  `integer`, `text` or `datetime`. Nothing undeclared can be stored: a metric or
  a field the schema does not name is rejected with 400 rather than ignored.
  Declaring a new one is a schema change (`PATCH /api/suites/{name}/schema`).
- **Machine** -- where a benchmark ran, addressed by `name`. Carries the
  declared `machine_fields` under `fields`, and a built-in `tracked` flag
  marking whether it takes part in *automatic* machine selection. Untracked
  machines are otherwise returned like any other.
- **Commit** -- what was benchmarked, addressed by an identity string `value`
  (a Git SHA, a version, or an ad-hoc label like `experiment-vectorizer-v2`).
  Two optional attributes matter: `ordinal`, an integer placing the commit in
  the suite's total order, and `tag`, a human label such as `release-18.1`. An
  ordinal is never inferred -- not even from a numeric commit string -- and a
  commit without one is grouped but has no position, so it is absent from every
  ordinal-ordered result.
- **Run** -- one submission of results for one machine at one commit,
  identified by a UUID. Several runs may share a machine and a commit.
- **Test** -- a benchmark name, created implicitly by submission. Test names
  legitimately contain `/`, so **no path ever carries one**: a request names a
  test in the `test=` query parameter or in a request body.
- **Sample** -- one measurement of one test in one run: `{test, metrics}`, where
  `metrics` holds only the metrics that have a value. A test measured several
  times in one run yields one sample per repetition.
- **Profile** -- optional instruction-level counter data for one test in one
  run, submitted inline with the run and read back through its own UUID.
- **Regression** -- a performance change someone is tracking: a title, a state,
  an optional suspected commit, free-form notes, and *indicators*, each naming
  one `(machine, test, metric)` the change was observed on. LNT does **no**
  detection of its own; an external analyzer reads the time series and records
  what it finds here.

## Conventions

Suite-scoped paths are written in full the first time and abbreviated
afterwards: anything below starting `/commits`, `/machines`, `/profiles`,
`/query`, `/regressions`, `/runs`, `/tests` or `/trends` hangs off
`/api/suites/{testsuite}/`.

- **No trailing slashes.** `/api/suites/` is answered with a 307 to
  `/api/suites`. The method and body survive the redirect, but save the round
  trip.
- **Lists are objects, never bare arrays**: `{"items": [...]}`, plus `"cursor":
  {"next": ..., "previous": null}` on a cursor-paginated list, or `"total": N`
  on an offset-paginated one, which takes `offset=` alongside `limit=`. `items`
  is present and empty when nothing matches. `/machines` is the only
  offset-paginated list; every other paginated list uses a cursor.
- **Cursors are opaque and forward-only.** Send `cursor.next` back unchanged,
  the way that list takes it -- as the `cursor=` query parameter, or as the
  `cursor` key of the request body for the lists that take a body -- alongside
  the same filters and `sort`. Never parse one. `previous` is always null.
  `limit` defaults to 25 and may not exceed 10000.
- **Sorting** is `sort=<field>`, with a `-` prefix for descending
  (`sort=-submitted_at`). Lists that take no `sort` are still in a stable order
  suitable for paging.
- **Errors** look like
  `{"error": {"code": "not_found", "message": "..."}}`. Branch on `code`, never
  on `message`. The one exception is a request body too large for the
  deployment, refused at the transport layer with a plain-text 413 and no
  envelope. The codes are `invalid_request` (400), `unauthorized` (401),
  `forbidden` (403), `not_found` (404), `duplicate`, `ordinal_conflict`,
  `in_use` and `conflict` (409), and `internal_error` (500). The four 409s are
  distinct because they call for different behaviour: a `duplicate` run UUID is
  worth retrying with a fresh one; an `ordinal_conflict` means your view of the
  commit order is wrong and retrying cannot help; an `in_use` means something
  else still references what you asked to delete, and has to go first; and a
  `conflict` is everything else, which needs reading the message: a submission
  contradicting stored metadata cannot be retried as sent, whereas one caused by
  a concurrent schema change can.
- **A filter naming something absent** has three different answers, on purpose:
  an unknown `machine=` or `test=` is 404, an unknown `metric=` is 400, and a
  `commit=` value no commit has is an empty page. A commit named as a *range
  bound* is the exception and is 404, because it names a position rather than a
  set of rows -- and 400 if it exists but has no ordinal, since then it sits
  nowhere in the order. Same for a commit named in a request body, which is 404.
- **Timestamps** are ISO 8601 in UTC with a `Z` suffix, in both directions.
  Values inside `fields` and `metrics` use the JSON form of their declared type
  and are never stringified.
- **References are mostly flat.** A run carries `"machine": "linux-x86_64"` and
  `"commit": "abc123"` -- the other entity's identifier, not a nested object --
  so resolve a page of commits in one call with `POST /commits/resolve`. Two
  things nest or denormalize instead, and say so: a commit's `previous`/`next`
  neighbours, and time-series points and trend items, which carry the commit's
  `ordinal` and `tag` so a point can be placed without a second call.

## Authentication

Send `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, where a token is 64 lowercase hex
characters. Scopes form a hierarchy -- `read` < `submit` < `triage` < `manage`
< `admin` -- and a key grants its own scope and every lower one.

- `read` covers every read endpoint but one, including the `POST`s that only
  query (`/commits/resolve`, `/query`, `/trends`), and **allows anonymous
  access**: if you only need to read, send no header at all. The exception is
  `GET /api/admin/api-keys`, which needs `admin` like the rest of that family.
- `submit` submits runs and creates commits; `triage` manages regressions;
  `manage` manages machines, commits, runs and suites; `admin` manages API keys.

The HTTP method implies nothing about the scope; the OpenAPI document records
what each operation needs. A header that is present but unreadable is 400 --
an absent header and a broken one are not the same thing -- an unknown or
revoked token is 401 even where anonymous access would have been allowed, and a
valid token with too little scope is 403.

## Workflows

**Find out what this instance holds.** `GET /api/suites` returns every suite
with its full schema, which is what tells you the metric and field names every
other call needs.

**Submit a run.** `POST /api/suites/{testsuite}/runs` (scope `submit`) with
`format_version: "5"`, a `machine` object, a `commit` object and a list of
`tests`, each entry a test `name` plus its metric values. A metric value may be
an array, which records one sample per repetition. The machine and the commit
are created if they do not exist; the run's own `uuid` is optional and is
generated when omitted. The whole submission is atomic. Two things to know:
`submitted_at` is always the server's, never yours, and submission never
overwrites stored metadata -- a field whose stored value differs from what you
send is 409 `conflict`, and `PATCH` is the only way to change it.

**Chart a metric over time.** `POST /api/suites/{testsuite}/query` (scope
`read`) with a body of `{metric, machine, test, commit, after_commit,
before_commit, after_time, before_time, sort, limit, cursor}`. Only `metric` is
required; `test` accepts a list. Each point carries its `value` along with the
commit's `ordinal` and `tag`, so it can be placed on an axis without a second
call. The response is cursor-paginated: keep sending `cursor.next` back in the
body until it is null.

**Get an overview across machines.** `POST /api/suites/{testsuite}/trends`
(scope `read`) with `{metric, machine, last_n}` returns one geomean per
(machine, commit) over the last `last_n` ordered commits, unpaginated. The
metric must be numeric. This is what a dashboard renders; `/query` is what a
single trendline needs.

**Follow up on a data point.** A point carries `run_uuid`. From there,
`GET /runs/{uuid}` gives the run and its `run_parameters`,
`GET /runs/{uuid}/samples?test=<name>` every metric that run recorded for a
test, and `GET /runs/{uuid}/profiles` the profiles it captured.

**Read a profile.** `GET /runs/{uuid}/profiles` lists `{test, uuid}` for each
profile the run captured, which is how a test name becomes a profile UUID.
Then `GET /profiles/{uuid}` gives the top-level counters,
`GET /profiles/{uuid}/functions` every function with its aggregate counters
sorted hottest first, and `GET /profiles/{uuid}/functions/{name}` the
disassembly with per-instruction counters. Only the last of those decompresses
anything, so ask for one function rather than all of them. A stored profile
that cannot be read is 500 `internal_error`; a function name the profile does
not hold is 404.

**Record a regression.** `POST /api/suites/{testsuite}/regressions` (scope
`triage`). Every field is optional: `title`, `bug`, `notes`, the `commit` you
suspect, and `indicators`, each `{machine, test, metric}`. The state starts at
`detected` unless the body says otherwise, and moves freely between
`detected`, `active`, `not_to_be_fixed`, `fixed` and `false_positive`
via `PATCH`. Indicators are added and removed in batches through
`/regressions/{uuid}/indicators`; a removal naming an indicator that is not
there is ignored rather than an error, so retrying one is safe.
